title: The order to turn the lights read at Comhairle nan Taighean-solais
summary: Comhairle nan Taighean-solais sits and hears the council's order that the five lights of the coast be turned to dubhan and their coal given to the altars. Taigh-solais Baile ìseal and Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg, nearest the works at Seann Skell, are to be turned first, in the summer; the keepers keep their warrants, wages and houses.

title: The custodians of Tobar dhearg ask for the flame
summary: The custodians of Tobar dhearg, who keep the light's log for Brìde's sake, ask the Àrd-choimheadaiche that the coal flame of their light be carried to Brìde's altar at Seann Skell and burn out there. He consents, and Comhairle nan Taighean-solais makes no objection, so long as the light is not dark a single night.

title: Ciorstaidh nic Artair refuses a deputy for the lantern
summary: Offered a clerk of the lights or a young custodian of Seann Skell to carry the flame the nine and a half miles to the altar, Ciorstaidh nic Artair, keeper of Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg, writes that the flame is hers by her warrant until the burner is lit, and that she will carry it herself. The answer leaves the matter to her.

title: Taigh-solais Baile ìseal turned to dubhan
summary: The burner Peigi nic Ascaill tried in the yard below Taigh-solais Baile ìseal is set in the tower's lantern by order, the first of the five lights to burn dubhan. Its keeper Seonag nic Thòmais, who would not have the thing up her stair, keeps the light under it.

title: The tank landed at the cape of Tobar dhearg
summary: A works boat from Seann Skell lands an iron tank, a burner, pipes and forty barrels of dubhan on the stones below Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg. Eight men of the village bring the tank up the landing-stones and the stair, and the barrels stand against the tower wall where the coal-sacks stood.

title: The trial of the burner at Tobar dhearg
summary: Peigi nic Ascaill lights the new burner in the lantern of Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg for an hour beside the coal grate. The light is white and steady and throws the shadows of the lantern's bars across the cape; the boats at sea come in to ask what has happened. The grate burns on alone until the day of the carrying.

title: The last coal night at Tobar dhearg
summary: On the night before the carrying the keeper of Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg burns the last of the quarter's coal, a sack and a half, as high as the grate will take it. At dawn she lights the closed lantern from the grate and lets the tower's fire go out.

title: The walk from the cape to Seann Skell
summary: Ciorstaidh nic Artair carries the lantern on foot from the cape by Baile gharbh to Seann Skell, nine and a half miles in the heat, and gives it to no one. Some thirty people of Tobar dhearg walk behind her with the three custodians of the village; at the town's edge a young custodian of the house leads her up to Brìde's house.

title: The first dubhan night at Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg
summary: On the evening of the carrying the under-keeper of Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg lights the dubhan burner at sunset, as the keeper ordered, with the keeper away at Seann Skell. The new light is seen white and steady from the quays of Seann Skell, nine miles up the coast.

title: The Àrd-choimheadaiche blesses the lantern
summary: When the coal flame of Tobar dhearg has burned out on Brìde's altar, Alasdair mac Ìomhair closes the lantern, says the words for a lamp of the vein's coal let go out, and blesses the lantern while he neither blesses nor forbids the new light. He gives the lantern back to its keeper at her asking.

title: The song of the last flame first sung at Seann Skell
summary: In a tavern under the quay wall at Seann Skell a skipper of Tobar dhearg makes and sings a song of the carrying on the night of it. It gathers many verses before morning, and by the summer's end every harbour of the south coast has its own; the first verse, of the flame gone out of the tower, is sung wherever it is sung.
